html:
Aquileia was founded in 181 BCE as a Roman colony at the head of the Adriatic Sea, in what is now northeast Italy. About three thousand families of settlers were sent to guard the frontier against the Gauls and the Istrians.

The site sat near the sea on a river, at the point where roads from Italy met routes over the eastern Alps. More settlers were added in 169 BCE. The town grew into a rich trading city. Amber from the Baltic came in along the Amber Road, and wine, oil and metal goods went out. Julius Caesar kept legions here in winter. By the 2nd century CE Aquileia was one of the largest cities of the empire, with perhaps 100,000 people.

Its position on the main road into Italy also made it a target. In 452 CE Attila and the Huns destroyed it. Survivors fled to the islands of the lagoon nearby, one of the beginnings of Venice. Aquileia's great early church, with its 4th century mosaic floor, still stands, and the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
